F23.quote: The AI Incident Tracker uses large language models (LLMs) to process incident reports from the AI Incident Database (AIID) and classify them along five taxonomies, producing standardized data that policymakers and researchers can use to track trends.
F23.claim: the method restated: LLMs classify AIID incident reports along five taxonomies, producing standardized data
F23.lineage: method: Arcola AI's LLM pipeline over AIID reports

F24.quote: Harm Severity (how serious the harm was, rated across 10 harm-types), EU AI Act Risk Level (the regulatory risk tier under the EU AI Act), Causal Taxonomy (what stage of the AI lifecycle the harm stems from and whether it was intentional), Domain Taxonomy (7 high-level categories of risks, such as discrimination or malicious use), and Subdomain Taxonomy (24 more specific subcategories within domains)
F24.claim: the five taxonomies: harm severity, EU AI Act risk level, causal, domain (7) and subdomain (24)

F25.quote: Because the tracker relies on automated LLM classification rather than manual review, we need to understand whether LLMs can classify incidents as consistently as expert humans. This report describes a pilot study to compare the performance of eight LLMs against expert human reviewers
F25.claim: the occasion of validation: automated classification without manual review; a pilot study of eight LLMs against expert reviewers

F26.quote: We asked two expert reviewers to independently read reports of 10 incidents and classify each one using five taxonomies … We selected 10 incident reports from the AI Incident Database.
F26.claim: the pilot's design: two expert reviewers, ten incidents, five taxonomies

F27.quote: Opus 4.6 and Kimi K2.5 were the two strongest models in our evaluation and met or exceeded the currently used model, Sonnet 4, on most taxonomies.
F27.claim: the model the tracker currently uses is Sonnet 4; Opus 4.6 and Kimi K2.5 met or exceeded it on most taxonomies

F28.quote: On the EU AI Act Risk Level taxonomy they performed substantially worse. … After targeted prompt refinement, Opus 4.6 matched or exceeded the human-human agreement baseline on all five taxonomies on this pilot sample.
F28.claim: the EU AI Act level was the weak taxonomy; after prompt refinement Opus 4.6 met the human baseline on all five, on the pilot sample

F29.quote: By the Landis & Koch interpretation scale, the human-human agreement is itself only "Fair" for Harm Severity (0.31) and "Moderate" for EU AI Act Risk Level (0.56).
F29.claim: the human baseline itself is only fair for harm severity (0.31) and moderate for EU AI Act level (0.56)

F30.quote: Incident reporting has contributed to major safety improvements in high-stakes sectors such as aviation, healthcare, and nuclear power
F30.claim: its premise: incident reporting improved safety in aviation, healthcare and nuclear power

F31.quote: Several databases already collect reports of AI-related incidents, including the AI Incident Database, the OECD’s AI Incident Monitor, the AIAAIC Repository, the Political Deepfakes Database, and others. The MIT AI Incident Tracker project builds on these efforts by classifying each incident against a set of risk taxonomies and rating the severity of the harm involved.
F31.claim: its place: built on the incident databases (AIID, OECD monitor, AIAAIC, Political Deepfakes Database), classifying each incident and rating its harm
F31.lineage: neighbours: the incident databases it builds on

F32.quote: These outputs have been used to report on incident trends, including in the 2026 World Disasters Report and Time magazine.
F32.claim: its uptake: used in the 2026 World Disasters Report and Time magazine

F33.quote: The Incident Tracker uses large language models (LLMs) to make incident classification scalable. … However, LLMs can make mistakes when interpreting incident reports and assigning classifications. For instance, they can occasionally hallucinate details and can exhibit a score-range bias, where ratings cluster within a narrow band of an ordinal scale rather than using the full range.
F33.claim: LLMs for scale; and their errors: hallucinated details and score-range bias

F34.quote: The human consensus labels used as the benchmark for evaluating LLM performance were based on a small review sample: two reviewers per incident across 10 incidents.
F34.claim: the pilot's stated limit: a small review sample

F35.quote: Our results suggest that LLM-based incident classification has comparable accuracy to the human baseline and is a viable approach for scaling the Incident Tracker. … The next step is to run a more comprehensive validation study based on this pilot. … The full set of reports from the AI Incident Database will be reclassified using the updated model selection and adapted prompts, to refresh the Incident Tracker with more reliable classifications.
F35.claim: its conclusion and plan: comparable accuracy, a fuller validation study next, and a reclassification of every AIID report

F36.quote: This brings us completely up to date with the latest incidents on the AI Incident Database as at 23 June 2025 (up to incident ID #1116)
F36.claim: on 23 June 2025 the tracker reached AIID incident ID #1116

F37.quote: The full dataset has been classified using this latest iteration of the tool (reclassification of all incidents that were classified with the previous version, to ensure consistency across the dataset).
F37.claim: every incident reclassified with the new iteration, for consistency

F38.quote: The harm severity analysis uses a new scale, simplifying scoring to 1-5 points (previously 0-10). … I have tried to remove ambiguities from the definitions in the scale and to make it possible to grade incidents consistently with greater objectivity.
F38.claim: the severity scale changed from 0–10 to 1–5, its definitions disambiguated (in the first person)

F39.quote: Assesses NatSec impact of each incident in 5 categories: Physical Security & Critical Infrastructure / Information Warfare & Intelligence Security / Sovereignty & Government Functions / Economic & Technological Security / Societal Stability & Human Rights using this framework. … Classifies threat for Imminence, Novelty and Autonomy
F39.claim: the five national-security categories and the threat classification
